what: Number to Words turns a number written in digits, such as 1,234.56, into English words, such as "One thousand two hundred thirty-four point five six". It also has a money mode that writes an amount the way it goes on a check or cheque, in the currency you pick: "One thousand two hundred thirty-four dollars and 56/100", or euros, pounds, rupees, riyals and more.

It helps when you write checks, invoices, contracts, receipts or legal documents where amounts must also appear in words, when teachers and students practise reading large numbers, and when you just want to know how to say a very long number. It handles whole numbers up to 18 digits, decimals and negative numbers.
The words are created in your browser as you type; nothing is sent to a server.
uses: Get the exact wording for the amount line of a check or cheque, with the cents, pence or paise written as a fraction.
Many formal documents state amounts in figures and in words to prevent mistakes or fraud.
See how large numbers are grouped into thousand, million and billion, or into lakh and crore, and where hyphens go.
Style guides often say to write numbers in words at the start of a sentence.
Find out how to say a number like 7,500,000,000 (seven billion five hundred million).
tutorial: Click the "Number" box and type digits, for example 1234.56. You can include commas, spaces or a currency sign; they are ignored. A comma used as the decimal point also works, so 1.234,56 and 12,5 are read the European way. A minus sign at the start makes the number negative.
The words appear in the box below at once and change with every key you press. The first letter is a capital so you can paste it at the start of a line.
Use "Write as". "Number" writes the whole number in words and reads each decimal digit one by one after "point", for example 3.14 becomes "Three point one four".
Use money mode for checks and cheques

Choose "Money amount (for checks and cheques)" and pick your currency. The whole part becomes the currency in words and the smaller unit is written as a fraction out of 100, for example 250.5 in dollars becomes "Two hundred fifty dollars and 50/100". Use no more than two decimal places; amounts like 9.999 are not rounded and show a message instead.

"Number style" uses thousand, million and billion by default. Choose "Lakh and crore (South Asia)" to get, for example, "Twelve lakh fifty thousand" for 12,50,000, as used in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal.
The whole-number part can have up to 18 digits, which reaches into the quadrillions (up to 999,999,999,999,999,999). Longer numbers show an error.
Click "Copy" to copy the words, then paste them into your check-writing app, invoice or document.
features: Words update as you type, with no button to press.
Writes the amount in words with the cents, pence or paise as a fraction, in dollars, euros, pounds, rupees, riyals, dirhams, naira, rand, pesos and more.
Reads decimal digits one by one after the word "point".
Adds "minus" in front of numbers below zero.
Handles thousand, million, billion, trillion and quadrillion.
Commas, spaces and currency signs are removed automatically, and a decimal comma such as 12,5 is understood.
An optional South Asian number style writes large numbers in lakh and crore.

example.title: Worked example: writing a rent check
example.text: Your rent is 1,850.75. Type 1,850.75 in the Number box. With "Write as" set to "Number" you see "One thousand eight hundred fifty point seven five". Switch to "Money amount (for checks and cheques)" with "Dollars and cents" and it becomes "One thousand eight hundred fifty dollars and 75/100". Write that on the long line of the check and draw a line through the empty space after it so nothing can be added.

tips: In money mode, an amount of exactly 1 uses the singular, such as "One dollar" or "One pound"; every other amount uses the plural.
Type a whole amount like 500 in money mode to get, for example, "Five hundred euros and 00/100".
Hyphens are used for numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine, as in standard American English.
Leading zeros are ignored, so 007 is read as seven.
If your currency is not in the list, use "Number" mode and add the currency name yourself.
problems: "Enter a number using digits, for example 1234.56."
The box contains letters or symbols other than digits, separators and currency signs. Type only digits, one decimal point or comma and an optional minus sign.
"That number is too large. The limit is 18 digits."
The whole-number part is longer than 18 digits. Shorten it or split it into parts.
"Money amounts can have at most two decimal places, for example 9.99. Round the amount first."
Money mode never guesses cents. A value like 9.999 or 4.567 has more than two decimals, so round it yourself and type, for example, 10.00 or 4.57. Extra zeros at the end, such as 4.500, are fine.

The cents are the first two decimal digits, so 4.5 becomes 50/100 and 4.05 becomes 05/100. Check that you typed the decimal point in the right place. A single comma followed by three digits, such as 1,500, is read as a thousands separator, not a decimal.
